title: The glass and the pour
lead: A clean glass and a proper head: what a guest sees first.

sections.name: Bottles, nitro and temperature

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Every beer has its pour and its temperature.

Nitro: pour three-quarters, let it settle, top up.
Lagers colder than ales; darker and stronger, warmer.

keyPoints.line: water coats a clean glass evenly.
rings of foam after each sip.

read.bigIdea: A dirty glass kills the head.
read.where: A **beer-clean** glass forms a proper head and leaves **lacing** as it’s drunk. Three checks from the Brewers Association: the **sheeting** test (dip it in water: a clean glass is coated evenly, a dirty one beads), the **salt** test (salt sticks evenly to a wet clean glass, not to greasy spots), and the **lacing** test (foam clings in **rings** after each sip). **Bubbles stuck** to the sides mean it isn’t clean.
read.mixup: A glass can look spotless and still not be beer-clean. Grease is invisible; the beer shows it.

keyPoints.line: no milk or egg-white glasses in the washer.

read.where: Wash in **three sinks**: warm water with a **sudsless** detergent and a brush, a **cold rinse**, then **sanitizer**. Dry glasses **upside down** on a rack, never with a towel. Keep a washer for **beer glasses only**: fat from creamy coffee mugs or **egg-white cocktails** coats glasses and kills the head. Rinse each clean glass in **cold water** just before filling. Skip **frozen or frosted** glasses: they cause foam and over-chill the beer.
read.mixup: A frosty mug looks cold and refreshing, but it foams the beer and hides its flavor.

keyPoints.line: tilt and pour down the side.

read.where: Hold the glass at **45°**, about an inch under the faucet, and **open it all the way**. Pour down the side, then **straighten** the glass and pour down the middle to build the head (Cicerone says straighten at about two-thirds full; the Brewers Association says about halfway). Close as the foam reaches the rim. Aim for about **1 inch** of head; German **wheat** beers and Belgian ales get **2–3 inches**. The faucet **never touches** the glass or the beer.

stops.name: Straighten
stops.text: Halfway to two-thirds, pour down the **middle**.

stops.name: Finish
stops.text: About **1 inch** of foam at the rim.

read.mixup: A head isn’t short-changing the guest: foam is part beer, and it carries the aroma.
read.sayIt: Here you go, poured with a proper head.

keyPoints.line: stop before it, unless the style wants it.
serve colder for lagers, warmer for dark and strong.

read.bigIdea: Know how each beer wants to be served.
read.where: A bottle with **yeast** in it: pour gently and stop when the yeast reaches the neck, unless the guest wants it or the style (like a **Weissbier**) is poured with it; when unsure, **ask**. **Nitro** beer: pour to about **three-quarters**, let it **settle 1–2 minutes**, then top up. Serve beer between **38 and 55°F**: **lagers colder** than ales, **darker and stronger** beers warmer.
read.mixup: Colder isn’t always better. Too cold numbs the taste and hides the aroma.
read.sayIt: Would you like the yeast in it, or poured clear?

sources: Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org); Cicerone, US Certified Beer Server Syllabus v6.0, 2024 (cicerone.org); American Homebrewers Association, “Proper Beer Serving Temperatures” (homebrewersassociation.org). Checked Nov 8, 2026.
